notable_claims: Drew University's 1989-1990 policy treats computer abuse as equivalent to the theft of other university property.
The author describes Drew's existing policy as 'from the 70's' and 'vague'.
classification.summary: Tom Limoncelli of Drew University requests that other institutions share their written computer use policies to create a comparative directory. He provides the existing policy from Drew University's 1989-1990 handbook as an example. The provided policy defines abuses such as unauthorized file entry, network access, and account sharing.
classification.title: Written Policies

notable_claims: NCSA policy granted the director the right to monitor email
Warning users of monitoring is insufficient justification for reading private mail
classification.summary: The author critiques the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) email policy that grants the director the right to monitor communications. The post notes that while NCSA requested suggestions for revising the policy from a university committee, the monitoring authority remained in place. The author argues that providing a warning about potential mail monitoring does not justify the act of opening it.
classification.title: Re: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom

identity.subject: Re: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom

notable_claims: Systems staff must not be held liable for the contents of messages on the system, otherwise they have an obligation to censor.
Academic freedom on computers should be consistent with academic freedom regarding physical bulletin boards and mail.
Administrative intervention is justified in cases of resource abuse, imminent danger (bugs/exploits), malware distribution, or illegal activity.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: Sanjay Kapur, a system administrator at SUNY Stony Brook, proposes specific policy guidelines for university computing services to balance academic freedom with system stability. He argues that systems staff should not be held liable for user content to avoid the necessity of censorship and suggests that electronic resources should be treated similarly to physical campus resources. The proposal outlines specific technical and behavioral triggers that justify administrative intervention or disciplinary action.
classification.title: Policy requirements to prevent chaos

notable_claims: Personal non-commercial use of university computers should be tolerated if costs are not substantially increased.
Universities and Congress should establish a legal right to email privacy analogous to telephone privacy laws.
Institutions should tolerate hypothetical legal risks associated with user content on email or Usenet.
Electronic publication via mailing lists and Usenet extends freedom of the press beyond print media.
classification.summary: John McCarthy outlines a proposed framework for institutional computing policies. He argues for the tolerance of personal non-commercial use, the establishment of email privacy rights, and the protection of electronic speech. He suggests that computers provide an opportunity to expand freedom of the press beyond traditional print media.
classification.title: What university (and other organization) policies should be

identity.subject: Computers and Academic Freedom mailing list (batch edition)

notable_claims: Intervening in the form of a post (e.g., excessive quoting or wrong newsgroup) is distinguished from censoring content or tone.
Inspecting notes before they are sent is characterized as prior restraint and inconsistent with academic freedom.
The moderation of Usenet newsgroups or mailing lists may technically fit the definition of censorship.
classification.summary: Rich Kulawiec defends his past actions as a system administrator who removed Usenet posts based on form and netiquette rather than content. The discussion explores the tension between maintaining shared computer resources and upholding academic freedom, specifically regarding prior restraint and censorship. Kulawiec acknowledges that by some definitions, administrative moderation of network traffic constitutes censorship.
classification.title: Replies to "Well, was I a censor?"

identity.subject: Replies to "Well, was I a censor?"

notable_claims: Strict limitations to 'academic' purposes for email are unworkable, unnecessary, and undesirable.
Personal development cannot be effectively segregated from personal purposes in a digital context.
classification.summary: Mitchell A. Pravatiner critiques a proposed email policy by Sanjay Kapur that sought to distinguish between 'university' and 'personal' account usage. Pravatiner argues that segregating personal development from personal purpose is impractical and that strict limitations on academic use are unworkable. He advocates for maximum individual latitude, suggesting that abuses should be handled on a case-by-case basis rather than through preemptive restriction.
classification.title: Why Kapur may be wrong on at least one count

identity.subject: Why Kapur may be wrong on at least one count

notable_claims: Distinguishes between 'personal development' and personal purposes (e.g., commercial use) in university computing policies.
Claims that Usenet is not a purely academic network and thus does not qualify for the protections of academic freedom.
Argues that providing access to Usenet news should be the responsibility of the local community rather than the University.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: Sanjay Kapur responds to Mitchell Pravatiner regarding the definition of acceptable use for university computing resources. Kapur argues that while 'personal development' should be broadly defined, it must be distinguished from purely personal purposes and resource theft. He further contends that Usenet is not a purely academic network and therefore does not merit the protections of academic freedom.
classification.title: Re: Why Kapur may be wrong on at least one count

classification.summary: James R. Bottum of the NCSA requested that a campus-wide committee review the center's email use and security policy following complaints from UIUC faculty. The correspondence indicates a conflict between administrative email policies and academic freedom. Carl Kadie notes that both students and faculty members objected to the policy.

George B. Trubow's IEEE Software column provides guidance for private corporations to eliminate employee privacy legally.

He argues that guidance from a 'Law Review' column in IEEE Software regarding private corporations is inapplicable to an academic environment. The post highlights a conflict between administrative monitoring of electronic communications and academic freedom.
